'''unpucker''' (un-puk′ėr), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''pucker.''] To smooth away the puckers of; relax.

{{smaller block|Let but Teufelsdröckh open his mouth, Heuschrecke’s also ''unpuckered'' itself into a free doorway.
{{right|''Carlyle'', Sartor Resartus, i. 3.}}}}

'''unpuff†''' (un-puf′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''puff.''] To take away the vanity of; humble.

'''unpunctually''' (un-pungk′t̮ụ̄-a̤l-i), ''adv.'' In an unpunctual manner; not punctually.

{{smaller block|<poem>To Phœbus, and in vain my light I lend,
Gaz’d on unto my setting from my rise
Almost of none but of ''unquiet'' eyes.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Maid’s Tragedy, i.}}}}

{{smaller block|A tumbrell or cucking-stool, set up . . . for the correction of ''unquiet'' women.
{{right|''J. Collins'', Hist. of Somersetshire (ed. 1791), III. 460.}}}}

'''unquiet<sup>2</sup>†''' (un-kwī′et), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''quiet.''] To disquiet.
{{smaller block|<poem>Here has fallen a business
Between your cousin and Master Manly has
''Unquieted'' us all.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Devil is an Ass, iv. 1.}}}}

'''unquietly''' (un-kwī′et-li), ''adv.'' In an unquiet manner or state; without rest; in an agitated state; uneasily.
{{smaller block|One minded like the weather, most ''unquietly''.
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iii. 1. 2.}}}}

'''unquietness''' (un-kwī′et-nes), ''n.'' The state of being unquiet; agitation; excitement; uneasiness; restlessness.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Iago.'' Is my lord angry?
''Emilia.'' He went hence but now,
And certainly in strange ''unquietness''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, iii. 4. 133.}}}}

'''unquietude†''' (un-kwī′e-tūd), ''n.'' Inquietude.
{{smaller block|A kind of ''unquietude'' and discontentment.
{{right|''Sir H. Wotton'', Education of Children.}}}}

'''unquit†''' (un-kwit′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unquit''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''quit.''] '''1.''' Not discharged; not freed from obligation.
{{smaller block|<poem>Gracinus, we must pray you, hold your guards
''Unquit'' when morning comes.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Sejanus, v. 5.}}}}

raw_text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|unprovable|6638|unquit}}</noinclude>Dissuasive from Popery.

'''unproved''' (un-prövd′), ''a.'' [< ME. *''unproved;'' < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''proved.''] '''1.''' Not proved; not known by trial; not tested.
{{smaller block|A fresh ''unproved'' knight.
{{right|''Spenser.''}}}}
'''2.''' Not established as true by argument, demonstration, or evidence.
{{smaller block|There is much of what should be demonstrated left ''unproved.''
{{right|''Boyle.''}}}}

'''unprovedness''' (un-prövd′nes), ''n.'' [ME. ''unprovedness;'' < ''unproved'' + ''-ness.''] Inexperience. ''Wars of Alexander'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1019.

'''unprovide''' (un-prọ̄-vīd′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''provide.''] To unfurnish; divest or strip of qualifications; in the following quotation, to divest of resolution.
{{smaller block|I’ll not expostulate with her, lest her body and beauty ''unprovide'' my mind again.
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, iv. 1. 218.}}}}

'''unprovided''' (un-prọ̄-vī′ded), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not provided; unfurnished; unsupplied: with ''with,'' formerly ''of:'' as, ''unprovided with'' money.
{{smaller block|Utterly ''unprovided of'' all other natural, moral, or spiritual abilities.
{{right|''Bp. Sprat.''}}
I shall make the public a present of these curious pieces at such time as I shall find myself ''unprovided with'' other subjects.
{{right|''Addison'', Frozen Words.}}}}
'''2.''' Having made no preparation; not suitably prepared; unprepared.
{{smaller block|<poem>Tears for a stroke unseen afford relief;
But, ''unprovided'' for a sudden blow,
Like Niobe we marble grow.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Threnodia Augustalis, v.}}}}
'''3†.''' Unforeseen. ''Spenser.''

'''unprovidedly''' (un-prọ-vī′ded-li), ''adv.'' In an unprovided manner; without provision; unpreparedly.

'''unprovident†''' (un-prov′i-dent), ''a.'' Improvident. ''Beau. and Fl.'', Thierry and Theodoret, iv.

'''unprovoked''' (un-prọ-vōkt′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not provoked; not incited.
{{smaller block|When all on the sudden, the Smectymnuans, a strange generation of men, ''unprovoked'', unthought of, cry out of hard measure, and fly in my face, as men wrongfully accused. {{right|''Bp. Hall'', Ans. to Vindication of Smectymnuus.}}}}
'''2.''' Not proceeding from provocation or just cause: as, an ''unprovoked'' attack.
{{smaller block|A rebellion so destructive and so ''unprovoked''. {{right|''Dryden.''}}}}

'''unprovokedly''' (un-prọ-vō′ked-li), ''adv.'' In an unprovoked manner; without provocation.

'''unprudence†''' (un-prö′dens), ''n.'' [ME.; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''prudence''.] Want of prudence; imprudence; improvidence.
{{smaller block|The ''unprudence'' of foolis [is] erring. {{right|''Wyclif'', Prov. xiv. 18.}}}}

'''unprudent†''' (un-prö′dẹnt), ''a.'' Imprudent.

'''unprudential''' (un-prọ-den′shạl), ''a.'' Imprudent.
{{smaller block|The most unwise and ''unprudential'' act. {{right|''Milton'', Eikonoklastes, xxiii.}}}}

'''unpruned''' (un-prönd′), ''a.'' Not pruned; not lopped or trimmed.
{{smaller block|Fruit-trees all ''unpruned''. {{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., iii. 4. 45.}}}}

'''unpublic''' (un-pub′lik), ''a.'' Not public; private; not generally seen or known. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Virgins must be retired and ''unpublic''. {{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Holy Living, ii. 3.}}}}

'''unpublished''' (un-pub′lisht), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not made public; secret; private.

{{smaller block|''Unpublish’d'' virtues. {{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iv. 4. 16.}}}}

'''2.''' Not published; still in manuscript, as a book.

{{smaller block|The finest Turner etching is of an aqueduct with a stork standing in a mountain stream, not in the published series; and next to it are the ''unpublished'' etchings of the Via Mala and Crowhurst.
{{right|''Ruskin'', Elements of Drawing, 1872.}}}}

'''unpucker''' (un-puk′ėr), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''pucker.''] To smooth away the puckers of; relax.

{{smaller block|Let but Teufelsdröckh open his mouth, Heuschrecke’s also ''unpuckered'' itself into a free doorway.
{{right|''Carlyle'', Sartor Resartus, i. 3.}}}}

'''unpuff†''' (un-puf′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''puff.''] To take away the vanity of; humble.

<poem>We might ''enpuff'' our heart, and bend our knee,
T’ appease with sighs God’s wrathfull Maiestie.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, i. 4.}}}}

'''unpunctual''' (un-pungk′t̮ụ̄-a̤l), ''a.'' Not punctual; not exact, especially with reference to time. ''Pope.''

'''unpunctuality''' (un-pungk-t̮ụ̄-al′i-ti), ''n.'' The state or character of being unpunctual. ''H. Spencer'', Study of Sociol., p. 285.

'''unpunctually''' (un-pungk′t̮ụ̄-a̤l-i), ''adv.'' In an unpunctual manner; not punctually.

'''unpunishable''' (un-pun′ish-a̤-bl), ''a.'' Not punishable; not capable or deserving of being ''ton'', Answer to Salmasius, v. 157.

{{smaller block|Where all offend, the crime ’s ''unpunishable.''
{{right|''May'', tr. of Lucan, v.}}}}

'''unpunishably''' (un-pun′ish-a̤-bli), ''adv.'' Without being or becoming liable to punishment. ''Milton'', Answer to Eikon Basilike, § 28.

'''unpunished''' (un-pun′isht), ''a.'' Not punished; suffered to pass without punishment or with impunity.

<poem>Shall innocence
In her be branded, and my guilt escape
''Unpunish’d?''</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Fletcher (and Massinger?)'', Lovers’ Progress, v. 1.}}}}

'''unpure''' (un-pūr′), ''a.'' Not pure; impure. ''Donne.'' [Rare.]

'''unpurely''' (un-pūr′li), ''adv.'' Impurely. ''Bp. Bale'', English Votaries, ii. [Rare.]

'''unpureness''' (un-pūr′nes), ''n.'' Impurity. ''J. Udall'', On Luke ii. [Rare.]

'''unpurged''' (un-pėrjd′), ''a.'' Not purged. (''a'') Unpurified.

{{smaller block|The rheumy and ''unpurged'' air. {{right|''Shak.'', J. C., ii. 1. 266.}}}}

{{smaller|(''b'') Not cleared from moral deflement or guilt.}}

{{smaller block|I feare it would but harme the truth for me to reason in her behalfe, so long as I should suffer my honest estimation to lye ''unpurg’d'' from these insolent suspicions.
{{right|''Milton'', Apology for Smectymnuus.}}}}

'''unpurposed''' (un-pėr′po̤st), ''a.'' Not intended; not designed.

{{smaller block|Accidents ''unpurposed.'' {{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., iv. 14. 84.}}}}

'''unpurse''' (un-pėrs′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''unpursen''; < ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''purse.''] '''1.''' To take out of a purse; expend. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|Ever was the gold ''unpursed.'' {{right|''Gower'', Conf. Amant., v.}}}} '''2.''' To rob of a purse or money. ''Pollok.'' [Rare.]

'''unpurveyed†''' (un-pėr-vād′), ''a.'' [ME., < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''purveyed.''] Unexpected; unforeseen.
{{smaller block|Hem that she [Fortune] hath left in dyspeyre, ''unpurveyed.'' {{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, ii. prose 1.}}}}

'''unqualified''' (un-kwol′i-fīd), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not qualified; not fit; not having the requisite talents, abilities, or accomplishments.
{{smaller block|The learned are held ''unqualified'' to serve their country as counsellors merely from a defect of opulence. {{right|''Goldsmith'', Vicar, xix.}}}}
'''2.''' Not qualified legally; not having the legal qualifications; specifically, not having taken the requisite oath or oaths; not having passed the necessary examinations and received a diploma or license: as, an ''unqualified'' practitioner of medicine.
{{smaller block|By the statutes for preserving the game, a penalty is denounced against every ''unqualified'' person that kills a hare. {{right|''Blackstone'', Com., I., Int., § ii.}}

In the course of time, through relaxation of bardic discipline, the profession was assumed by ''unqualified'' persons, to the great detriment of the regular bards. {{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', VII. 791.}}}}
'''3.''' Not modified or restricted by conditions or exceptions; absolute: as, ''unqualified'' praise.
{{smaller block|That women and children taken in war, and such men as have not been slain, naturally fall into ''unqualified'' servitude, is manifest. ''H. Spencer'', Prin. of Sociol., § 456.}}

'''unqualifiedly''' (un-kwol′i-fīd-li), ''adv.'' In an unqualified manner; without qualification; absolutely.

{{smaller block|Him of Cyprus, to whom the Syriac versions ''unqualifiedly'' attribute them. {{right|''Amer. Jour. Philol.'', VIII. 91.}}}}

'''unqualifiedness''' (un-kwol′i-fīd-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being unqualified.

{{smaller block|The advertency and ''unqualifiedness'' of copiers. {{right|''Bibliotheca Biblica'', I. 65. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}}

'''unqualify''' (un-kwol′i-fī), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''qualify''.] To divest of qualifications; disqualify. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|Deafness ''unqualifies'' me for all company. {{right|''Swift.''}}}}

'''unqualitied†''' (un-kwol′i̤-tid), ''a.'' Deprived of the usual qualities or faculties.

{{smaller block|He is ''unqualitied'' with very shame. {{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., iii. 11. 44.}}}}

'''unquantified''' (un-kwon′ti-fīd), ''a.'' Not quantified.—'''Unquantified proposition.''' See ''proposition''.

'''unquarrelable†''' (un-kwor′el-a̤-bl), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''quarrel''<sup>1</sup> + ''-able''.] Incapable of being quarreled with, objected to, or impugned.

{{smaller block|Such satisfactory and ''unquarrelable'' reasons. {{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Vulg. Err., vi. 10.}}}}

'''unqueen''' (un-kwēn′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''queen''.] To divest of the dignity of queen. [Rare.]

<poem>Although ''unqueen’d'', yet like
A queen, and daughter to a king, inter me.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., iv. 2. 171.}}}}

'''unquenchable''' (un-kwen′cha̤-bl), ''a.'' and ''n.'' '''I.''' ''a.'' Not quenchable; incapable of being quenched, extinguished, allayed, or the like: as, ''unquenchable'' fire, thirst, etc. {{smaller block|activity of the ''unquenchable'' passions of human nature.
{{right|''Maudsley'', Body and Will, p. 168.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' That which cannot be quenched; figuratively, one whose zeal cannot be quenched. [Colloq.]

'''unquenchableness''' (un-kwen′cha̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The state of being unquenchable. ''Hakewill'', Apology, iv. 4.

'''unquenchably''' (un-kwen′cha̤-bli), ''adv.'' In an unquenchable manner; so as to be unquenchable.
{{smaller block|That lamp shall burn ''unquenchably.''
{{right|''Scott'', L. of L. M., ii.}}}}

'''unquestionability''' (un-kwes″chọn-a̤-bil′i-ti), ''n.'' The character or state of being unquestionable; also, that which cannot be questioned or doubted; a certainty.
{{smaller block|Our religion is . . . a great heaven-high ''Unquestionability.''
{{right|''Carlyle'', Past and Present, ii. 6.}}}}

'''unquestionable''' (un-kwes′chọn-a̤-bl), ''a.'' '''1.''' That cannot be questioned or doubted; indubitable; certain: as, ''unquestionable'' evidence or truth; ''unquestionable'' courage.
{{smaller block|King Henry the Seventh being deceased, his only Son Prince Henry . . . by ''unquestionable'' Right succeeded in the Crown, at the Age of eighteen Years.
{{right|''Baker'', Chronicles, p. 254.}}}}
'''2.''' Averse to being questioned; averse to conversation.
{{smaller block|An ''unquestionable'' spirit, which you have not.
{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, iii. 2. 393.}}}}

'''unquestionableness''' (un-kwes′chọn-a-bl-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being unquestionable; unquestionability.

'''unquestionably''' (un-kwes′chọn-a-bli), ''adv.'' Without doubt; indubitably.
{{smaller block|At fit howr [Anacktus] setts on alone toward the Camp; is mett, examin’d, and at last ''unquestionably'' known.
{{right|''Milton'', Hist. Eng., i.}}}}

'''unquestioned''' (un-kwes′chọnd), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not called in question; not doubted.
{{smaller block|It is the sober truth of history, ''unquestioned'', because unquestionable. {{right|''Story'', Speech, Salem, Sept. 18, 1828.}}}}
'''2.''' Not interrogated; having no questions asked; not examined; not examined into.
{{smaller block|<poem>It prefers itself and leaves ''unquestion’d''
Matters of needful value. ''Shak.'', M. for M., i. 1. 55.</poem>}}
'''3.''' Not to be opposed or disputed.
{{smaller block|Their ''unquestioned'' pleasures must be served.
{{right|''B. Jonson.''}}}}

'''unquestioningness''' (un-kwes′chọn-ing-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unquestioning; unquestioning action. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|The new men . . . have come to be accepted . . . with . . . cordial ''unquestioningness''. {{right|''The Century'', XX. 3.}}}}

'''unquick''' (un-kwik′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not quick; slow. ''Imp. Dict.''—'''2†.''' Not alive or lively. ''Daniel'', Civil Wars, iii.

'''unquiescence''' (un-kwī-es′e̤ns), ''n.'' Disquiet; inquietude.

'''unquiet<sup>1</sup>''' (un-kwī′et), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''quiet''.] Not quiet; not calm or tranquil; restless; agitated; disturbed; also, causing disturbance.
{{smaller block|<poem>For almost all the world their service bend</poem>}}
<poem>To Phœbus, and in vain my light I lend,
Gaz’d on unto my setting from my rise
Almost of none but of ''unquiet'' eyes.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Maid’s Tragedy, i.}}}}

{{smaller block|A tumbrell or cucking-stool, set up . . . for the correction of ''unquiet'' women.
{{right|''J. Collins'', Hist. of Somersetshire (ed. 1791), III. 460.}}}}

'''unquiet<sup>2</sup>†''' (un-kwī′et), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''quiet.''] To disquiet.
{{smaller block|<poem>Here has fallen a business
Between your cousin and Master Manly has
''Unquieted'' us all.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Devil is an Ass, iv. 1.}}}}

'''unquietly''' (un-kwī′et-li), ''adv.'' In an unquiet manner or state; without rest; in an agitated state; uneasily.
{{smaller block|One minded like the weather, most ''unquietly''.
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iii. 1. 2.}}}}

'''unquietness''' (un-kwī′et-nes), ''n.'' The state of being unquiet; agitation; excitement; uneasiness; restlessness.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Iago.'' Is my lord angry?
''Emilia.'' He went hence but now,
And certainly in strange ''unquietness''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, iii. 4. 133.}}}}

'''unquietude†''' (un-kwī′e-tūd), ''n.'' Inquietude.
{{smaller block|A kind of ''unquietude'' and discontentment.
{{right|''Sir H. Wotton'', Education of Children.}}}}

'''unquit†''' (un-kwit′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unquit''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''quit.''] '''1.''' Not discharged; not freed from obligation.
{{smaller block|<poem>Gracinus, we must pray you, hold your guards
''Unquit'' when morning comes.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Sejanus, v. 5.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
